principles.text: Hire people who give a shit: caring doesn't guarantee great work, but not caring guarantees bad work.
Find the neglected bottleneck: many people worked on algorithms and chips, nobody on data, so Scale built the data layer.
Keep teams small and talent-dense. Big teams ship less than small teams, not just per capita but overall.
Build conviction in beliefs nobody else shares; if you go too much with the herd, you will get immensely confused.
Don't outsource product thinking to public benchmarks; build your own evals and set launch-blocking thresholds.

sampleQA.question: How do I keep the hiring bar high as we scale?

answer.text: Screen for two things: caring about the company's mission and caring about work in general. Past obsession predicts future obsession.
Ask "What's the hardest you've ever worked on something?" He calls it an extremely efficient filter.
Don't hire by brand. A spotless track record of high-brand companies can signal risk aversion and not sticking through adversity.
Rapid headcount growth erodes the bar. Hold the team small while the business grows, and approve hires yourself.

sampleQA.question: When is an AI agent product ready to ship?

answer.text: List 100+ specific behaviors, set a launch-blocking threshold for each, and ship only when all are green. For Muse, 80 green rows and 20 red ones wasn't good enough.
Judge it with internal evals for what users value, not viral public benchmarks.
Avoid the "self-driving trap": shiny demos rarely reach 100% production reliability within a few years.
For personal agents, reliability is the product. Unreliable experiences make users churn.

sampleQA.question: My market looks small. Should I still go after it?

answer.text: Yes. Start in almost the narrowest market you can, build momentum, then grow out toward bigger markets.
How fast the market grows and whether you can dominate it matter more than the size of the TAM.
Every important company had a small TAM when it started; get in before the area is cool to build a head start.
